newsitem.title: USA: New home starts, consumer sentiment show strength.
newsitem.headline: New home starts, consumer sentiment show strength.

text.p: Builders broke ground on more new homes last month than in March and consumer confidence rose in May, reports said Friday, underscoring the economy's strength as prospects of higher interest rates loom.

The data -- showing stronger-than-expected gains in construction starts and a record high reading for a barometer of consumer confidence -- were the last major reports before a meeting of Federal Reserve policy-makers on Tuesday.

The Commerce Department said construction starts on new homes and apartments rose 2.6 percent in April to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.47 million as a flurry of building in the South helped boost overall activity.
March starts were revised to show a 7.7 percent drop to 1.43 million, the department said.

In another report, consumer confidence showed strength, according to a survey by the University of Michigan. Its May index of consumer sentiment set a record when it rose to 104.6 from 101.4 in April, people who have seen the report said.
Home building in April outstripped Wall Street predictions that starts would rise at a rate of 1.43 million a year.
Much of the gain was driven by starts on apartment buildings. New building in that sector jumped 10.9 percent after rising just 0.9 percent in March.

But a big drop in permit applications for structures with more than five units signals that strength in that area could prove temporary, according to Dave Seiders, chief economist at the National Association of Home Builders.

Construction starts on single-family homes rose 0.3 percent in April to a rate of 1.12 million after falling 9.9 percent in March. Total starts during April were 3.2 percent lower than they were in April 1996.

"Today's numbers are moderate in part because the warm weather ... allowed some of these starts to get going (in March)," said Paul Taylor, senior economist at America's Community Bankers, a Washington-based trade group.

In addition, mortgage rates have drifted lower since early April, which may have given a boost to new building. The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said rates on 30-year loans averaged 7.91 percent this week, down from 8.18 percent on April 3.
Still, builders are concerned Fed policy-makers will nudge short-term interest rates up another quarter percentage point when they meet next week, as they did at their last meeting in March.
Interest rates affect not only consumers' ability to carry mortgages but also builders' costs to break ground.
But economists remained divided about whether the Fed will move to raise short-term rates next week.
"It's a really, really close call right now," Seiders said. "They know all they're going to know."

Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal chief economist Tim O'Neill said the housing starts data increased the likelihood that the Fed will raise the federal funds rate a quarter point next week "to address continued upside risks to inflation."

But others say reports earlier this week showing a big drop in wholesale inflation, tame inflation on the consumer front and flat industrial output could put the Fed in somewhat of a bind as it weighs the possibility of a rate increase.

"The inflation data will make it politically difficult or impossible for the Fed to raise rates," said Ken Mayland, chief economist at KeyCorp in Cleveland. "One could argue the Fed should have the luxury of waiting."
The April homebuilding report showed starts jumping in the South, the nation's biggest regional housing market, by 11.3 percent to the highest rate since July 1995, after a 6.4 percent drop in March.

Starts in the Midwest climbed 0.7 percent after dropping 24.9 percent in March. Starts fell 7.4 percent in the Northeast after a 9.6 percent gain and in the West, starts fell 6.5 percent after a 1.9 percent March rise.
